content: The draft documents relevant to the deliberations of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) were distributed to meeting participants two weeks prior to the meeting to allow for their review and comments. During the meeting, these documents were revised to incorporate the participants' deliberations and feedback. After the meeting, members of the WHO Steering Group prepared a comprehensive guideline document to accurately reflect the discussions and decisions made by the participants. This draft was then electronically sent to the GDG and the External Review Group (ERG) for their final review and approval. Following the GDG's approval, the finalized document was sent to eight independent external experts, who were not part of the guideline panel, for peer review. The WHO Steering Group evaluated the feedback from these peer reviewers to determine which inputs should be included in the final document. Post-meeting and external peer review, the WHO Steering Group made only factual corrections and language improvements to enhance clarity. The WHO recommends the use of oxytocin (10 international units [IU], administered intramuscularly or intravenously) for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) in all births. In cases where women giving birth vaginally already have intravenous access, the slow intravenous administration of 10 IU oxytocin is preferred over intramuscular administration. This recommendation is based on evidence showing that intravenous oxytocin reduces the risk of PPH, severe PPH, blood transfusion, and severe maternal morbidity, with no significant differences in undesirable effects compared to intramuscular administration. However, routine intravenous oxytocin use may require additional resources, potentially impact women's comfort, and increase health inequities. The feasibility of intravenous administration may vary depending on the setting. The GDG emphasized that intravenous access should not be routinely established solely for the administration of intravenous oxytocin for PPH prevention. They also noted that previous trials for this indication used a 10 IU dose of oxytocin intravenously, with injection speeds ranging from 1 minute (bolus injection) to 40 minutes (infusion) and dilution volumes ranging from 1 mL to 1000 mL of saline. While no direct evidence compares different regimens for intravenous oxytocin administration during vaginal birth, observational studies in women undergoing cesarean sections suggest that rapid intravenous administration can cause harmful hemodynamic effects. Therefore, the GDG recommends avoiding rapid injections and prefers that the 10 IU dose be diluted and administered slowly. The GDG acknowledged existing WHO recommendations against the routine use of intravenous fluids during labor and childbirth, emphasizing the unnecessary costs and resource use associated with this practice in many health facilities. They reiterated that intravenous access should not be routinely established for the sole purpose of administering intravenous oxytocin for PPH prevention. The dissemination and implementation of this recommendation require collaboration among stakeholders at international, national, and local levels. It is essential to increase women's access to maternal health care and strengthen the capacity of health-care facilities to provide high-quality services. The recommendation will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, and other relevant entities. It will also be made available on the WHO website and translated into the six United Nations languages. National and subnational subgroups may adapt and implement this recommendation based on existing strategies, including revising national guidelines or protocols. The adaptation process should aim to improve the quality of maternal health care and achieve the best possible outcomes for women and their babies. This process should also consider the unique needs of women in emergency settings, including their values and preferences. Oxytocin should only be administered by skilled health personnel trained in the safe use of injectable uterotonics. While oxytocin is relatively inexpensive and widely available, it requires cold chain storage (2–8 °C) to maintain its quality and efficacy. In settings where cold chain storage cannot be guaranteed, the effectiveness of oxytocin may be compromised. Programs implementing uterotonics for PPH prevention should ensure that women are adequately informed about the need for uterotonics, available options, potential side effects, and their right to choose their care. Health systems must ensure the availability of quality-assured uterotonics and necessary equipment at all maternity service locations. This includes establishing robust regulatory, procurement, and logistics processes to ensure the correct storage and transportation of medicines. Procurement agencies should only source quality-assured oxytocin labeled for storage at 2–8 °C in single-use ampoules or vials of 10 IU/mL. Despite some manufacturer labeling suggesting stability at room temperature, oxytocin should always be refrigerated to prevent degradation and maintain quality. The GDG identified knowledge gaps requiring further research, particularly regarding the optimal effective regimen of intravenous oxytocin for PPH prevention after vaginal birth. Implementing this evidence-based recommendation will require resources for sustainable procurement and storage of uterotonic drugs, as well as training for health-care providers. Standardizing care by incorporating this recommendation into existing care packages can encourage behavior change among health-care providers. Potential barriers to implementation include a lack of skilled personnel, resistance to adopting evidence-based practices, inadequate infrastructure, and insufficient supplies and equipment. Strategies to address these barriers are outlined in the implementation considerations. Monitoring and evaluating the implementation and impact of this recommendation will be conducted at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality.
